transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Redwood Solutions), Liam O'Connor (Avalon Head of ML), Priya Shah (Avalon Infra), Ethan Brooks (Avalon CTO), Zara Kim (Avalon SRE)

Summary: short technical deep dive into tail latency. Focus on why p99 spikes under peak concurrent streaming. Lots of kernel/quantization/batching talk, some network hop troubleshooting. Action items captured.

Topics: p99/p95 differences, streaming vs non-streaming timelines, KV cache impact, continuous batching and batch sizing, quantization and mixed-precision, VPC network hops, on-prem vs hosted differences.

00:00 Jamie Chen: ok hi everyone thanks for joining we're gonna dig into the p99 tail that you reported, quick intros pls
00:06 Liam O'Connor: yeah thanks jamie, i'm liam head of ml at avalon, priya on infra and zara our sre, ethan is here too
00:12 Jamie Chen: great, ravi and may a from our side, quick agenda - root causes, microbenchmarks, proposed mitigations, next steps, sound good?
00:20 Ethan Brooks: yep, real quick context, we run a mix of streaming chat and batch generation for document summarization, target p95 ~200ms, p99 ideally <450ms but we've seen spikes above 1.2s during bursts
00:40 Ravi Patel: ok that aligns with what i saw in the telemetry you shared - lots of small- QPS spiky patterns, and some requests are streaming so the network and chunk flush intervals can affect p99
01:02 Priya Shah: to be clear we're on a VPC peered connection to the hosted prod region, and also evaluating a private on-prem deployment for compliance - so network hops matter for us
01:20 Jamie Chen: perfect, so first let's scope the sources: model compute variance, kernel jitter, batching behavior, KV cache misses, and network egress/peering. we'll go through each with examples
01:40 Ravi Patel: starting compute - when you quantize to int8 or nf4 it reduces compute but can change kernel selection, sometimes causing a different attention kernel with slightly higher variance at specific seq lengths. we saw this on another customer where p95 improved but p99 got worse due to jittery kernel switching
02:10 Liam O'Connor: that's interesting - we did quantize a couple of models for cost, but maybe we missed a profile step
02:20 Ravi Patel: yep profiling is key. the runtime picks kernels based on seq len and batch shape. if you have heterogeneous sequence lengths streaming in, that can force less optimal kernels mid-run
02:50 Zara Kim: we noticed p99 spikes happen more when mixed streaming + batch jobs are running on the same node pool, could that be batching contention?
03:05 Ravi Patel: absolutely, continuous batching trades off latency and throughput. if batch windows expand under contention you get higher per-request latency. Redwood's continuous batching has policies to cap max batch wait and to prioritize low-latency routes
03:28 Maya Lopez: also caching - the KV cache prefix hits are huge for chat. if you get cache misses early in a conversation you pull more tokens, more KV throughput, and that can increase tail latency
03:44 Priya Shah: when you say KV cache misses are you referring to remote KV storage or the in-GPU KV cache? we've got a hybrid architecture with a small in-gpu cache and then a backing store in networked NVMe nodes
04:05 Ravi Patel: good call - we mean both. in-GPU KV is fastest; misses that spill to backing store incur I/O and network hops. in your topology with peered VPC and NVMe nodes, those extra hops can easily add 50-200ms depending on congestion
04:28 Ethan Brooks: that matches our numbers - the SREs saw additional 80-150ms correlated with disk reads on miss patterns
04:40 Jamie Chen: ok let's walk through a concrete scenario: streaming chat with 4 concurrent users, mixed seq lengths, 32-token streams. Request enters, hits router, if pinned to a node with cold KV the first streaming chunks will experience miss penalties
04:58 Ravi Patel: and the runtime handles KV cache insertion asynchronously, but the first couple tokens still wait. also note RPC serialization for streaming vs non-streaming differs - streaming keeps an open socket with frequent small frames; non-streaming waits to flush full response. TCP vs HTTP/2 chunking timing can affect p99
05:25 Liam O'Connor: any suggestions at infra level to mitigate? we can tune MTU, reduce number of network hops, pack NVMe closer or go to private deployment
05:38 Ravi Patel: yes reduce hops and colocate KV backing to the same AZ reduces variance. for stricter SLAs we recommend Dedicated capacity (reserved GPU pools) or Private deployment so you control placement and avoid noisy neighbors
06:01 Priya Shah: we were hoping to stay hosted but committed to a strict p99 SLA for a vertical customer - dedicated might be the path then
06:12 Jamie Chen: exactly - dedicated reduces multi-tenant jitter and gives predictable throughput; plus you can pin model variants and quantization profiles per pool
06:25 Maya Lopez: on the software side we recommend: 1) more aggressive prefix KV caching for hot convos, 2) tail-aware batching policies that shrink max batch time under high percentiles, and 3) use streaming with server-side chunk coalescing for small frames
06:50 Ravi Patel: I want to call out kernel selection again - if your quantized model triggers a fallback kernel for certain lengths you'll see long tails. we can run a kernel heatmap to show which sequence lengths map to which kernels and their timing
07:10 Liam O'Connor: yeah please run that - we saw weird spikes at seq len ~128 and 256 boundaries
07:18 Ravi Patel: that's typical; padding/rounding to power-of-two internal sizes can change perf characteristics. we'll profile those exact seq lengths
07:32 Zara Kim: about streaming vs non-streaming, we noticed non-streaming endpoints had lower p99 for long outputs but worse p95 for short quick requests. is that expected?
07:46 Ravi Patel: yes non-streaming batches responses which amortizes overhead, so throughput-friendly but introduces queuing delays for short requests. streaming reduces head-of-line latency but suffers from more small-packet overhead and network scheduling jitter
08:05 Ethan Brooks: any tips on batch sizing? we tried fixed small batches but saw underutilization, fixed large batches hurt latency
08:17 Maya Lopez: autotune. Redwood supports workload-aware batching with dynamic max batch sizes and latency SLO guardrails. start with conservative max batch wait 10ms, target batch size of 8, then stress test and tune by p95/p99 metrics
08:38 Liam O'Connor: we also use a prior model for reranking which adds extra KV lookups between steps, could that compound tail latency?
08:48 Ravi Patel: yes multi-stage pipelines multiply tail risks. consider caching reranker features and materializing intermediate KV entries so you don't re-read from disk each request
09:00 Priya Shah: can you explain how quantization changes cache behavior? we thought quantization was only compute related
09:10 Ravi Patel: quantization changes matrix math representation and sometimes memory layout; that can affect kernel footprint and memory bandwidth. with smaller model activations you might fit more in L2/L3, which helps, but the runtime may use different kernel algorithms that have different memory access patterns affecting KV throughput indirectly
09:34 Jamie Chen: network-wise, there are a few concrete measurements: one RTT across peering in your region is ~8-12ms, but NVMe node reads + serialization add 40-120ms per miss in your reported runs
09:50 Zara Kim: and spikes correlate with backup jobs and noisy IO on the backing nodes at midnight which then re-appears during backups across zones
10:02 Ravi Patel: that's a classic noisy-neighbor on storage. you can mitigate with QoS on NVMe, move backing store to provisioned instances, or adopt ephemeral in-GPU KV warmup for hot keys
10:22 Liam O'Connor: regarding on-prem, if we move to private deployment would Redwood still support remote telemetry and console?
10:30 Jamie Chen: yes Private keeps control plane optional - you can have a customer-managed control plane integrated with Redwood console for telemetry via secure peering and SAML SSO. audit logs and KMS integrations are supported as well
10:45 Ethan Brooks: good. security team will want to review SOC2 docs and network architecture before any trial
10:50 Jamie Chen: we will share SOC2, encryption at rest docs, and our VPC peering checklist. Maya will drop the docs
11:00 Maya Lopez: noted, will send.
11:06 Liam O'Connor: curious about p95 vs p99 when using streaming + chunk coalescing, is there empirical guidance?
11:14 Ravi Patel: empirically chunk coalescing reduces small packet overhead so p95 improves; p99 often depends on those edge cases where KV miss + kernel fallback + network congestion align. the histogram matters - if p99 is 3-5x p95 you have systematic tail events to address
11:36 Priya Shah: what's the best way to measure kernel fallback freq? do you need custom builds?
11:42 Ravi Patel: no custom builds. we can run a kernel heatmap profiler on your model on our runtime, it logs kernel IDs, seq len, and latency. we'll correlate with your telemetry to highlight fallback frequency
11:58 Ethan Brooks: excellent. also the edge case of TLS handshake churn for short-lived streaming connections adds noise - we should check keepalives and connection pooling
12:10 Zara Kim: we'll look at TCP keepalive and eBPF measurements to show retransmits and RTOs.
12:22 Jamie Chen: ok let's capture concrete mitigations and owners
12:28 Liam O'Connor: 1) move hot KV to in-GPU warmup, 2) run kernel heatmap, 3) try dedicated pool for a week of load testing
12:40 Ravi Patel: we'll also try tail-aware batching policy and stream chunk coalescing as mitigations to keep p99 down
12:52 Maya Lopez: and we'll collect microbenchmarks for quantized vs fp16 for your seq lengths 64/128/256
13:06 Priya Shah: timeline - we need a report to share with procurement by 2026-03-20; can we get initial numbers earlier?
13:17 Jamie Chen: yes action items to hit 2026-03-12 for microbenchmarks and 03-07 for initial benchmark sheet. we'll prioritize the kernel heatmap first
13:30 Ethan Brooks: any caveats about quantization and accuracy/regression? we can't degrade client-facing quality too much
13:38 Ravi Patel: we'll include evals on your test prompts and surface any quality regression. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles that balance latency and quality
13:50 Liam O'Connor: and can you simulate multitenant noisy neighbors? that's where our spikes seem to come from
13:58 Ravi Patel: yes we can run noisy neighbor emulation and force IO contention to see tail behavior; dedicated avoids that entirely by design
14:10 Jamie Chen: all right wrapping up - recap next steps and owners
14:15 Liam O'Connor: thanks everyone

Recap:

- Kernel heatmap profiling for seq lengths 64/128/256 (Ravi)
- Share Redwood latency benchmarking spreadsheet and previous customer p95/p99 runs (Jamie)
- Send SOC2/security pack and VPC checklist (Maya)
